title: Air Canada’s expanded route deal with United Airlines could lead to higher prices, watchdog warns

 Comments Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create an account Air Canada’s AC-T plan to co-ordinate with United Airlines UAL-Q on 10 cross-border routes would lead to higher prices for travellers, the Competition Bureau said in a report to the Minister of Transport released on Wednesday. 
 The two airlines have a long-standing co-operation arrangement, collaborating on prices, schedules, capacity and revenue-sharing on several routes. However, the airlines’ recent proposal to expand their arrangement violates their 2012 antitrust agreement with the competition watchdog that restricts co-ordination on the routes, the bureau said in its report. 
 The proposed routes would link Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa and Vancouver with Chicago, Cleveland, Denver, Houston, New York, San Francisco and Washington.
 Air Canada spokesman Christophe Hennebelle said the partnership with United has allowed Canadian travellers to reach more destinations in Canada and the United States. Since 2022, the airlines have launched 20 new routes and jointly carried more than 4.3 million passengers, Mr. Hennebelle said in an e-mail. 
 The Competition Bureau submitted its report as advice to Steven MacKinnon, the minister who is conducting a public-interest assessment of the airlines’ proposal and has the authority to veto it. 
 The watchdog said it conducted a new assessment of the routes and concluded the airlines’ co-operation “would lead to material anti-competitive effects, including price increases resulting in millions of dollars in consumer harm annually.”
 The bureau also found other airlines were unlikely to fly the same routes, given high barriers to market entry, and Air Canada and United would likely not face any competition. “As a result, the proposed arrangement would create or reinforce monopoly or near-monopoly conditions on several routes,” the bureau said. 
 “Competition between airlines helps keep fares lower and gives travellers more choice and better service,” Jeanne Pratt, interim commissioner of competition, said in a statement. “Our review found that allowing Air Canada and United to coordinate on these routes would likely reduce competition on key Canada-U.S. routes and lead to higher prices for travellers.”
 The bureau published a study in 2025 that concluded Canada’s domestic airline industry is dominated by Air Canada and its smaller rival, WestJet Airlines. At Canada’s major airports, the two carriers combined market share is 50 per cent to 75 per cent, the study found, linking a lack of competition with higher prices. 
 The comment period for the minister’s public-interest assessment of the expanded Air Canada-United arrangement is open until Nov. 15.
